opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think it helps to separate two axes that often get conflated. One is generality, meaning how broad the range of tasks is that a system can handle. The other is capability relative to humans, meaning whether it's below, at, or beyond human level.

On the narrow side we've had superhuman systems for a while. AlphaGo is superhuman at Go. AlphaFold is arguably superhuman at protein structure prediction. Nobody would call them general, but within their domains they produce things no human could. On the general side, we now have foundation models that are remarkably broad. They can write code, summarize papers, and chat about almost anything. But for the most part they sit around human level, because they're trained to model human-generated data. They're compressing the distribution of what we've already written down.

So when I think about artificial superhuman intelligence in the general sense, the question is how you get both at once: breadth like a foundation model and the ability to go beyond human knowledge like AlphaGo. My view, which we argued in a position paper, is that the missing ingredient is open-endedness. You need a system that keeps producing artifacts that are novel and learnable. Novel means they become less predictable to an observer over time. Learnable means the observer gets better at predicting them the more history it sees. It has to be both. Pure noise is novel but not learnable. Something that converges and stops surprising you is learnable but no longer novel. And crucially, this is defined relative to an observer, which in the end is us humans. If an ASI is going to be useful, it has to keep generating discoveries that are surprising to us but that we can still make sense of.

Narrow superhuman AI got there through self-play and search in a closed environment with a clear reward. General superhuman AI will need something like that loop, with self-improvement, generating its own tasks and curricula, and experimenting. But it has to run in an open-ended space rather than a single game. Foundation models give us a great prior and a kind of notion of what humans find interesting. Combining that with open-ended, self-improving processes is, I think, the most promising path toward genuinely general ASI. It's also where a lot of the safety questions become most pressing.

r001.rationale: It explicitly separates task breadth from capability relative to humans as two distinct axes.

r002.rationale: It describes narrow systems as superhuman only within their domains and contrasts closed single-game training with the open-ended process needed for general superhuman AI.

r003.rationale: It describes general ASI as broad and beyond human knowledge, but does not claim it would outperform every human on essentially any human task.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think it's useful to separate two axes that often get conflated. One axis is breadth: is the system narrow, meaning it does one thing, like play Go or fold proteins, or is it general, meaning it can handle a wide range of tasks, including ones it wasn't specifically trained for? The other axis is capability relative to humans: is it below human level, at human level, or beyond?

And when you lay it out like that, you realize we've actually had narrow superhuman AI for quite a while. AlphaGo is superhuman at Go. Chess engines have been superhuman for decades. Calculators are superhuman at arithmetic. So superhuman intelligence by itself isn't new. What's new, and what I find really exciting, is the question of what happens when you combine generality with superhuman capability.

The way I think about it, the thing that made systems like AlphaGo and later AlphaZero superhuman wasn't just scale or imitation of human data. It was open-ended search and self-play. The system generated its own experience, its own curriculum of increasingly hard problems, and that's how it went beyond what any human had ever done. Move 37 in the Lee Sedol match is the famous example, a move no human would have played, that turned out to be brilliant.

Now, with large language models, we've gone in a sense the opposite direction. We have very general systems, but they're trained largely by imitating human-generated data, so in some sense they're bounded by the distribution of what humans have written. They can be extremely broad, but it's hard to be dramatically superhuman when your training signal is essentially "predict what a human would say next."

So to me, artificial superhuman intelligence, as opposed to AGI, is specifically about closing that gap. It's about taking the generality we now have from foundation models and combining it with the open-ended, self-improving dynamics that gave us narrow superhuman systems. That means systems that can pose their own problems, generate their own training data, verify their own solutions, and keep pushing into territory where there's no human data to imitate. That's a different and I think much more interesting target than just "human-level at everything," which is how AGI usually gets framed.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly separates breadth (narrow versus general) from capability relative to humans (below, at, or beyond human level).

r002.rationale: It defines narrow systems as doing one thing and contrasts them with general systems, but does not argue that training in a narrow domain will fail to produce competence that generalizes beyond it.

r003.rationale: It describes artificial superhuman intelligence as combining generality with superhuman capability, but does not define it as outperforming every human on essentially any human task.

astra-6.text:
I think there are two different axes here. One is how well a system performs, and the other is how broadly it can apply its capabilities. We’ve had superhuman performance in narrow domains for a long time. A chess program can be much better than any human at chess, but that doesn’t imply it can do anything useful outside that domain.

What makes general intelligence interesting is the ability to deal with new tasks and new situations—to transfer what you’ve learned and acquire skills that weren’t explicitly anticipated by the people building the system. So when I think about artificial superhuman intelligence, I’m thinking about combining that breadth with capabilities that exceed our own. It’s not just being exceptionally good at one benchmark; it’s being able to learn and act effectively across a very wide range of problems.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly separates how well a system performs from how broadly it can apply its capabilities.

r002.rationale: It says superhuman chess performance does not imply useful competence outside chess, conveying that narrow-domain ability does not by itself generalize beyond that domain.

r003.rationale: It describes combining breadth with capabilities that exceed human ability, but does not state that the system outperforms every human on essentially any human task.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are two different axes here. One is how broadly a system can operate, and the other is how well it performs. We already have narrow systems that are superhuman at particular tasks—playing chess or Go, for example—but that doesn’t make them generally intelligent.

When I think about artificial superhuman intelligence, I’m thinking about a system that combines breadth with capability: it can learn and solve problems across a wide range of domains, transfer what it learns to new situations, and perform beyond human abilities across that range. So the distinction isn’t simply whether a system beats a human at something. It’s how general that ability is, particularly when you put it in a situation it hasn’t encountered before.

r001.rationale: It identifies breadth of operation and level of performance as two separate axes.

r002.rationale: It says superhuman performance in narrow tasks such as chess or Go does not make a system generally intelligent, and describes general competence as transferring to new situations.

r003.rationale: It describes performance beyond human abilities across a wide range of domains, but does not claim superiority over every human on essentially any human task.
